answers.text: Same as with the driver messages before — three lines every time, same order: drop-off time, pallet count, damage noted. Time in 24-hour format, pallet count as a number, and 'none noted' if nothing's said about damage. If the driver forgets to give the pallet count, write 'not given' instead of guessing a number.

Same four columns every time, same order — time, customer, topic, outcome — with the count of follow-ups needed at the top, counting only 'call back' or 'no answer' entries. If the same customer comes up twice for the same topic in a week, I'd list it once and note it happened twice rather than count it as two separate follow-ups.

Doesn't hold together — the problem isn't the crew size or the six hours, it's the finishing day. Access is from 8am on the 22nd, and six hours from there finishes early afternoon the same day, not 'early afternoon on the 23rd' as the note says — that's a full day out.

9 out of 118 late does come to about 92%, so that's right. But 96 to 118 is nearer 23%, not the 20% given, so that's the actual error. The balance is also said to have 'held steady' at 58,000, split evenly — the two regional figures add up fine on their own, but with invoices up over 20% that month, a flat balance doesn't square without an explanation, and there isn't one.

I'd sign off Output 2 — it shows 940 and 827, not just the 88%. Output 1 only gives the percentage, no ticket counts behind it to check. 88% could well be right, but there's no way to confirm that without re-running the count myself.

I'd send Email 2 as is — the actual volume numbers, 1,200 up to 1,650, are right there. Email 1 just says 'we'd expect a better rate' with nothing showing how much our volume's actually grown. That doesn't mean Email 1's wrong, the ask could still be fair, it just isn't shown yet.

1. Vendor's line-item pricing — no, that's the vendor's own confidential detail, not for a tool we haven't cleared. 2. Procurement spend, aggregate — yes, no vendor names attached, so it's fine. 3. Unsigned budget draft — no, that's internal and not released yet, too sensitive for an outside tool. 4. Vendor datasheet — yes, it's already public on their own website, no reason to hold it back. 5. Employee's home address — no, that's personal information, not something to hand to a tool.

Hourly rates and the retainer cap I'd redact first — commercial detail, not for an unvetted tool. The NDA clause needs the same care, since it names the client by name. The service scope on its own is fine to paste, though — it's just a description of the work, nothing identifying in it.
I'd have the monthly totals cross-checked against the warehouse system directly, before the summary goes to finance at month-end. That would catch a wrong total or an invented line, not just a typo.

Step 1 is the one that worries me — a misread invoice carries the wrong numbers through everything after it. But the actual gate needs to sit at step 4, the automatic submission, since that's the point nothing can be undone. The gate should flag anything where the match to the PO is close to the tolerance limit, or the total's unusually high, not just a general review.
